summary: Extends the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol so that link-specific PPP options can be negotiated properly. Because L2TP puts a virtual link between two PPP peers, they lose direct knowledge of the physical media, and these extensions help them negotiate options suited to it.

eli5.summary: When a tunnel hides the real wire, the two ends can no longer see what kind of cable is there. This note adds a way to pass that information along so they can still agree on settings.

subtitle: New L2TP messages let the tunnel ends agree on PPP link settings that depend on physical media only one end can see.

tldr.problem: When L2TP tunnels PPP frames, the tunnel end that negotiates PPP options (the LNS) cannot see the physical media the call arrived on, so it may pick options the link cannot actually support.
tldr.mechanism: The LAC sends two new AVPs, LCP Want Options and LCP Allow Options, inside ICCN or OCCN messages to guide LCP negotiation, and the LNS reports the negotiated LCP packets back in two more new AVPs carried in a Set-Link-Info message.
tldr.outcome: It adds four AVP attribute numbers (49 to 52) to L2TP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3437 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the base L2TP specification in RFC 2661.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP, RFC 2661) carries Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) frames through a tunnel. The tunnel has two ends: the LAC (L2TP access concentrator), where the native PPP link physically arrives, and the LNS (L2TP network server), at the far end of the tunnel.

The base L2TP specification tells the LNS very little about the interface a call came in on: only whether it was synchronous or asynchronous, and digital or analog. This document defines a more robust way to inform the LNS of what the LAC needs, and to inform the LAC of the LCP options that were negotiated. The RFC expects deep knowledge of RFC 1661 (PPP) and RFC 2661 (L2TP).
sections.eli5: One end of a tunnel can see the real wire and the other cannot. This note gives them a way to share what the wire needs.

sections.title: Why Proxy LCP Is Not Enough
sections.content:
L2TP already has Proxy LCP, which lets options be negotiated where the native PPP link resides. That avoids problems with options such as ACCM and Alternate FCS, which the LNS would not know how to negotiate without access to the physical media.

Proxy LCP brings its own problems. Some options should be set or adjusted by the LNS, such as the PPP authentication type and the MRU. Also, the PPP client may restart LCP negotiation at any time, and unless the LAC inspects every PPP data packet it forwards, it would not even notice.
sections.eli5: Letting the near end make all the decisions has a catch: the far end has opinions too, and the near end might not notice when the talk starts over.

sections.title: Three Kinds of LCP Options
sections.content:
The RFC sorts LCP options into roughly three categories by how they affect L2TP:

  • Options that affect framing in a way the LAC may need to handle, such as ALT-FCS, ACCM and MRU.
  • Options that are mostly transparent to the LAC, such as AUTH-TYPE.
  • Options the LAC may wish to influence because they depend on the media type, such as ACFC and PFC.

The document is most concerned with the first and third categories. LCP option information is carried the same way as the Proxy LCP AVPs in RFC 2661: a PPP LCP Configure-Request or Configure-Ack packet is encapsulated inside an L2TP AVP.
sections.eli5: Some settings change how the data is packed, some do not matter to the near end, and some depend on the kind of wire. This note cares most about the first and third kinds.

sections.title: LCP Want Options (Attribute 49)
sections.content:
The LCP Want Options AVP, attribute type 49, carries a list of options the LAC wants the LNS to negotiate. It is sent in ICCN or OCCN messages, and the RFC says it SHOULD be present in them. The Vendor ID is the IETF Vendor ID of 0, the AVP MAY be hidden, and its length before hiding is 6 plus the length of the LCP Configure-Request.

If the sender does not want a connection to a peer that does not understand the extension, it SHOULD set the M bit to 1; otherwise the M bit MUST be 0. The value is identical to the information field of a PPP LCP Configure-Request, and the LNS should use these suggestions when building its initial Configure-Request.

For the common options, the LNS SHOULD begin negotiation with the value given. For MRU, it MAY reduce the value if necessary. For ACCM, it may add bits while negotiating. For FCS-ALT the value has no consequence to the LNS, since the FCS is stripped at the LAC, but some PPP media types require the option.
sections.eli5: The near end hands the far end a wish list: start the conversation with these settings, please.

sections.title: LCP Allow Options (Attribute 50)
sections.content:
The LCP Allow Options AVP, attribute type 50, lists the options the LAC will allow the LNS to negotiate. It has the same layout and the same Vendor ID, hiding and M bit rules as Want Options, but it MAY (rather than SHOULD) be present in ICCN or OCCN. Its value is an LCP Configure-Ack style option list.

If an option is not listed, the LNS can assume the LAC does not understand how to perform it at the link layer and would Configure-Reject it. The information should be used when building PPP Configure-Ack, Configure-Reject and Configure-Nak messages. The LNS may accept an MRU reduction or ACCM bits, may accept PFC and ACFC, and for FCS-ALT SHOULD accept only the types listed.

If the LAC sends the AVPs from the Want or Allow sections, it MUST be prepared to accept the AVPs reporting results from the LNS.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what the near end can live with. Anything missing from the list is off limits.

sections.title: Reporting Results Back to the LAC
sections.content:
RFC 2661 already defines Last Sent LCP Confreq (attribute 27) and Last Received LCP Confreq (attribute 28), which go from the LAC to the LNS for Proxy LCP. To report negotiated LCP parameters in the other direction, this RFC defines two AVPs of precisely the same format: LNS Last Sent LCP Confreq (attribute 51) and LNS Last Received LCP Confreq (attribute 52).

When the LNS completes LCP negotiation, it MUST send a Set-Link-Info control message containing these AVPs, holding the last sent and last received LCP packets from the LNS point of view. New attribute numbers are used instead of reusing 27 and 28 because some existing L2TP implementations might see known AVP types in an unexpected place and raise a false error.

The AVPs from the LAC may coexist with the Proxy LCP and Proxy Authentication AVPs. If proxy AVPs arrive, the LNS may accept them or renegotiate LCP using the suggestions here. A LAC that wants to force LCP negotiation at the LNS should simply omit all Proxy AVPs. By default the new AVPs are not mandatory (M bit 0); setting M to 1 is NOT recommended unless operating without them is completely unacceptable.
sections.eli5: When the far end finishes agreeing on settings, it sends a report back so the near end knows what was decided.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC finds no known additional significant threats. The new AVPs identify link characteristics and interface information of a tunneled PPP link, so someone who snooped them could learn more about a network or its topology. The document argues this is no more than what may already be sent in PPP LCP packets over the tunneled link, just in a different form.
sections.eli5: Someone listening in could learn a bit about the wire, but they could already learn the same thing another way.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document requires four new L2TP AVP attribute numbers from IANA: 49 for LCP Want Options (Section 2.1), 50 for LCP Allow Options (Section 2.2), 51 for LNS Last Sent LCP Confreq and 52 for LNS Last Received LCP Confreq (both Section 2.3).
sections.eli5: Four new numbered slots are reserved in the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

messages.label: ICCN or OCCN
messages.note: May carry LCP Want Options (49) and LCP Allow Options (50).

messages.label: Set-Link-Info
messages.note: Carries LNS Last Sent (51) and LNS Last Received (52) LCP Confreq after LCP negotiation completes.
